[DAY4 11:48:00 - DAY4 11:51:00]
I first took out the trash by tossing it into a garbage bag, then went to the grill and poured water onto it to extinguish any embers. After picking up chopsticks and a bowl, I noticed Katrina washing dishes, then headed inside to turn on my phone and scroll through it. During this time, I engaged in brief conversations with Alice, Shure, and Katrina about eggs and other topics, maintaining awareness of the ongoing kitchen activities. This sequence completed the initial cleanup and transition from outdoor to indoor setting.

Inside the living room, I leaned against a doorframe holding my phone while chatting with Tasha. She suggested playing chess or Mahjong, prompting me to inquire about retrieving the Mahjong set from the bedroom. Accompanied by Tasha and joined by Lucia and Alice, we discussed how to access the Mahjong table, with Tasha guiding me to lift a lid to reach it. While Tasha examined the table, I checked the time on my phone and helped by lifting the frame from the side, coordinating with Shure who joined us while eating eggs. We conversed about the table's secret placement as I inspected a shelf in the yard, indicating progress toward setting up the Mahjong game. This event consolidated our plan to organize a group game and explored practical steps to access necessary equipment.

Following this, I observed social interactions in the living room where Tasha leaned against a door frame, Katrina played with her hair, and Shure suggested leaving the Mahjong table setup for later. Lucia and Katrina discussed flower pressing and blooming status of peonies and carnations, while Shure used a phone nearby and Tasha sorted trash. I entered the bedroom to unplug a data cable from the computer, then exited to collect trash from the table and handed it to Shure. Joining Alice and Lucia's conversation about the wilting peony, I inquired about ripening it quickly and joked about rapid blooming. This event reflected ongoing household management tasks, flower care discussions, and waste disposal coordination among the group.

I resumed tidying by picking up the pepper shaker and grinder from the barbecue grill while holding a data cable, then handed the pepper items to Shure. He urged me to finish “that thing,” referring to his graduation project report, which he said had only a small part left. I encouraged him to do a live thesis presentation. I then secured the trash bag and disposed of it, walked into the bedroom to set down the data cable, and saw Shure picking up the trash bag. Exiting, I approached Katrina at the table, who was examining a pressed flower pattern. I asked if it was pressed out, and she humorously noted it was squished. Shure commented on the pattern's different style, likening it to fireworks, while Katrina focused on the design. This final event combined completion of cleaning tasks, support for Shure’s academic work, and observation of creative activities involving pressed flowers.

[DAY3 20:33:00 - DAY3 21:33:00]
The group began collaborative food preparation involving multiple cooking tasks, scientific method discussions, and coordinated roles. Tasha and Lucia managed stirring and mold pressing, while I actively handled utensils, cut paper, and assumed responsibility for cutting the cake later. After supporting indoor cooking, I transitioned outside to discuss with Shure how to handle burned food pieces, marking a shift from direct cooking involvement to external coordination. This initial phase established task division and the collaborative environment for subsequent activities.

Returning indoors, I entered the kitchen where Tasha prepared food near the oven fire. Wearing heat-resistant gloves, I placed items into the preheated oven to start baking. I reviewed baking instructions with Tasha, confirming a 40-minute baking time and scheduling the timing for whipping cream accordingly. During this, Shure inquired about the event’s end date, to which I responded with plans to dismantle on Monday. After this brief discussion, I left the building while monitoring messages on my phone, signaling a momentary pause in direct kitchen involvement.

Inside the kitchen again, I joined Shure near the oven to plan charcoal ignition using a controlled live patch and water, intending to ignite alcohol upon the rider’s arrival. I asked about gasoline use for ignition; Shure confirmed its suitability but noted its absence onsite. I offered to borrow gasoline from home. Tasha questioned the setup’s effectiveness, and Shure reassured that alcohol was expected soon. Shure then invited us to set the table for eating, indicating the event was moving into the dining phase. This exchange clarified fire-starting methods and transitioned the group toward meal consumption.

Moving indoors, I received snacks and began eating while observing Tasha demonstrate kitchen tool use for moving and slicing cake layers. I volunteered to cut a potato and engaged in discussions about fillings and their preparation. Tasha collected everyone’s preferences for the fillings, and Katrina expressed enjoyment, establishing a communal food preparation and consumption rhythm. This phase combined practical cooking tasks with group input on food choices.

Preparing to cook mango, I consulted Tasha on peeling and cutting instructions but first left to retrieve alcohol and takeout from the alley. Upon returning to the courtyard, I greeted Shure and stored the items. Shure located charcoal tongs and a clip to prevent spills; I assisted in organizing these tools to ensure readiness before lighting the charcoal. I then ignited the charcoal by sprinkling alcohol onto it, managing minor spills while Shure cautioned about fire risks. This completed the ignition phase necessary for cooking. The event advanced from ingredient preparation to active fire management.

I received alcohol from Shure and offered to get drinks. Alice asked about the alcohol’s arrival, confirmed by Shure and me. Despite multiple attempts, we failed to light a fire indoors using paper and cardboard, leading to a discussion about purchasing a lighter as a backup. As I moved into the kitchen, Shure explained topics including Paramecia and password retention. With Alice’s help and Shure’s guidance, the cardboard was finally ignited. I carried it outside to the dining table, ate snacks, and then took eggs into the kitchen. Following Tasha’s instructions, I beat the eggs, separated yolks and whites, and continued until achieving the desired consistency, assisted by Lucia and Tasha. This segment involved troubleshooting ignition, knowledge exchange, and egg preparation.

I prepared eggs by cracking them into a bowl, discarding shells, and washing utensils as instructed. After wiping the bowl, I checked on the fire outside the oven. Shure explained that alcohol was causing combustion and clarified that paper, not charcoal, was burning. Agreeing with Shure’s proposal, I placed cardboard under the fire to control it. I re-entered the kitchen and resumed task management with Tasha’s trust, reflecting coordinated fire management and utensil handling. This event highlighted controlled fire maintenance and continued food preparation.

Checking Tasha’s preparations down the hall, I confirmed to Lucia that the outdoor grill was ready despite incomplete fire ignition. After Katrina’s arrival, I snacked while listening to Tasha and Lucia finalize portion planning. I offered to handle mango preparation, photographed Tasha, washed my hands thoroughly, and assisted with assembling the base. After washing hands again, I joined Tasha and Lucia in whisking the egg mixture. At Tasha’s instruction, I poured the mixture into molds, filling them 70-80% full and dividing into 12 portions. I then turned off the computer room light and returned to the kitchen, where we awaited baking completion while inspecting mangoes and monitoring oxidation. This event encapsulated portion planning, hygiene practices, and continuous monitoring during baking.

I began mango preparation by retrieving a knife and cutting board from Tasha and the cabinet. I washed the knife and my hands thoroughly before rinsing and cutting the mango on the counter. During this, Tasha, Katrina, and Lucia discussed chocolate nearby. I continued slicing the mango despite offers of help, then confirmed with Lucia the exclusion of garlic flavor before inspecting and washing the fruits again as Tasha and Katrina brought lettuce. This established the initial fruit and salad ingredient preparation phase, integrating individual task focus with group ingredient management.

Next, I took over pouring the egg mixture into containers, carefully distributing it evenly while receiving feedback from Tasha and Katrina. After finishing, I whisked the remaining mixture and placed the containers near the oven to prevent moisture loss, noting the kitchen’s limited space, which Lucia agreed with. We then waited for baking completion, during which I updated Tasha and Lucia on outside progress and prepared for the subsequent phase. This event involved precise portion handling and ongoing coordination amid spatial constraints.

I prepared the fire setup outside by assembling materials and attempting to light charcoal with alcohol, facing difficulty until Tasha announced the fire was lit. I cleaned the area while we discussed oxygen contact and material distribution, concluding the fire preparation as coordinated and complete. Meanwhile, I continued whisking and adjusting the egg mixture texture, following Tasha and Shure’s advice on handling and flipping techniques to improve consistency and softness. This phase combined fire preparation with refinement of egg mixture handling based on expert input.

While shaking and handling vegetables, I adhered to Tasha’s guidance on preserving specific parts for later use and coordinated with Lucia on professional handling methods, maintaining collaborative workflow. I then struck and inspected an object to remove bubbles, discussing its condition with Tasha and Lucia. After pausing due to difficulty, I resumed the task, demonstrating hands-on problem-solving with their input. This event emphasized detailed vegetable handling and problem resolution through team collaboration.

I briefly transitioned to placing a drawing on the wall, conversing with Lucia and Tasha about its qualities before returning to kitchen tasks. I resumed cutting mangoes, consulting Tasha for cutting technique and coordinating with Lucia to retrieve plates, while Tasha worked on oven setup. During cutting, Lucia washed dishes and discussed cleaning challenges; I arranged cut fruit as Tasha cleaned plates and demonstrated mango-eating methods. This concluded the fruit preparation phase through shared tasks and coordination. The event balanced art placement with continued food preparation and cleanliness.

I ate remaining meat and mango, cleaned my hands, and resumed cutting new mangoes around the seed while discussing dishes and roasting with Lucia and Tasha. I maintained caution when slicing, heeding their reminders about safety and iodine use, while managing spills and dirt on the oven tray as they advised cleaning methods. This completed mango preparation and confirmed readiness to proceed with subsequent cooking steps. The event focused on safe knife handling, cleanliness, and preparation finalization.

Engaging with Alice, Lucia, Shure, and Tasha, I washed and peeled mangoes, exchanging comments on cutting techniques, tools, and seasoning options. We coordinated readiness for eating and lighting needs, including discussions on lighting equipment and BBQ setup, such as placing a flashlight on a stand to compensate for extension cord limitations. I adjusted cutting direction accordingly as the conversation evolved. This event integrated ingredient preparation with logistical planning for lighting and dining.

Entering the computer room, I observed the surroundings and took over rack control from Lucia while conversing with her and Tasha. We addressed phone battery depletion and accidental frame drops, discussed alternatives for phone holders, and planned to gather more materials before moving outdoors. Outside, I joined Alice and Shure at the grill, noted power absence, then discovered a power socket, prompting quick action to reconnect wiring upstairs and improve lighting with Shure’s assistance. This event combined technical troubleshooting, resource management, and preparation for outdoor activities.

At the barbecue site, I organized and connected wires, adjusted lamp positioning, and documented Alice’s baking process with photos and videos. After sanitizing my hands, I joined the group to distribute skewers and manage limited food portions, coordinating with Tasha, Lucia, and Shure as eating commenced. We discussed utensil shortages, attempting to locate knives and chopsticks but found none suitable. We decided to proceed using available chopsticks and improvising with scissors, acknowledging the need for proper cutting tools. This phase focused on setup finalization, documentation, and resource improvisation during dining.

Finally, I began cutting the cake under Tasha’s instruction, managing heat and precision with support from Tasha, Lucia, and Katrina. After the initial cut, Tasha peeled a layer from the pot base for tasting. I measured and cut three cake layers, adjusting alignment with assistance and lightening the task by sampling the cake bottom as advised. Throughout, the team provided feedback and encouragement, and I completed the layered cake cutting with their support and active collaboration. This concluding event encapsulated coordinated cake cutting and tasting, marking the culmination of food preparation efforts.

[DAY3 19:33:00 - DAY3 20:33:00]
I collected and organized all portable power sources from multiple rooms, systematically unplugging phone chargers, power banks, and charging cables. Starting by unplugging a phone charger and placing items on a table, I proceeded through bedrooms and stairwells to gather all power banks, consolidating them into boxes and onto furniture for efficient management. This ensured that all devices were accounted for and ready for subsequent setup.

Next, I set up camera equipment across the rooms by connecting the collected power banks to charging cables and positioning them near cameras in various locations such as sofas, flower pots, and floors. After each connection, I verified camera status via my phone, moving through areas including the kitchen to monitor device operation. This process ensured all cameras were powered and correctly positioned for recording.

I then managed power banks and cameras by sequentially plugging power banks into camera cables, turning cameras on, and verifying functionality through unplugging and replugging cables as needed. Using my phone, I scanned QR codes to align cameras, standing on stools to hold codes up to cameras while moving through the kitchen. Continuous monitoring of camera statuses confirmed all devices were operational and properly configured.

Controlling camera functions remotely, I scanned QR codes from the sofa and initiated communication by launching WeChat and sending messages via my phone. I connected a laptop with a data cable, checked phone call status, and alternated between keyboard and touchpad operation while multitasking with my phone. Additional cables were plugged into the computer, system status monitored, and equipment functionality confirmed, ensuring integrated device control.

I initiated communication with Lucia by interacting with the laptop, then walked to knock on her bedroom door before sitting on the sofa to discuss. During the conversation, I reviewed camera footage on my phone and coordinated a recording plan involving wearing glasses and simulating a phone call. This aligned team efforts and clarified task execution.

Afterward, I checked power banks by pressing buttons to confirm charge status, placing one on the sofa before lying down to continue laptop work. Later, I shifted to operate a second computer. I answered a phone call instructing the caller to put on glasses, held a power bank, and returned to laptop use. Moving through rooms, I checked equipment and waved at cameras before descending to the first floor, where I observed colleagues preparing food and engaged in brief interactions, including eating a strawberry and speaking with Alice.

Meeting with Alice and Lucia, we discussed completing the task quietly without waking a sleeping individual. We confirmed the person was unresponsive to knocking and agreed to proceed with tidying. I checked power bank charge levels, charged one for Alice, and discussed usage plans with Lucia. Our main objective was to follow the person preparing desserts, accepting limitations without their cooperation. Alice questioned AI understanding, prompting a brief exchange in which I confirmed AI knowledge.

At the stairwell, I informed Alice we could not go upstairs and began descending. After confirming knocking had been done properly, we proceeded downstairs. On the first floor, I entered the kitchen and inquired about tasks. Shure directed me to bring items, marking a transition to active kitchen work.

In the kitchen area, I observed and participated in food preparation. The team discussed ingredient storage and cooking methods such as grilling oysters and baking mangosteen. I picked up and ate fruit during the process while the group coordinated handling ribs, water bottles, and cooking wine. Shure requested assistance filming hand movements. Planning included baking potatoes for dinner and enhancing dishes with cooking wine, supporting meal preparation.

I engaged in light conversation about flavors, secret recipes, and culinary traditions while helping prepare ingredients alongside the team. The dialogue covered cooking excellence and innovation, with recognition of Shure’s progress and originality. This phase emphasized collaborative cooking efforts and thematic reflections.

We planned outdoor grilling, discussing food types and scheduling some tasks for Sunday, including roasting and eating protocols. I confirmed grilling would occur outside where lighting was limited. Together with Alice and Lucia, I assessed outdoor lighting, noting five wall lights and darker areas. We verified that studio lights and fire-starting methods using paper would suffice for the cooking event.

Back inside, I observed ongoing food preparation, including Tasha eating pizza, and received honey from Alice. We discussed washing lettuce, peeling potatoes, opening bottles, and kitchen organization. I inspected a pot and participated in trash sorting as part of cleanup. The team coordinated final preparations and cleaning to support the meal, concluding organized setup and readiness for cooking and filming tasks.

I disposed of trash by placing the garbage bag in the bin, shaking it, and carrying the can outside to leave the bag in a courtyard corner. Returning indoors via the living room to the kitchen, I observed Alice organizing the trash can and Tasha picking up a basin. I proceeded to the poolside faucet to fill and clean a pot. During cleaning, a discussion arose about cooking oysters: Shure insisted on adding oil despite grilling directly without brushing. Frustrated, I discarded oysters and continued cleaning. Unable to find steel wool, I went upstairs to the second-floor kitchen, found and rinsed steel wool near the pool, returned downstairs, and scrubbed the pot thoroughly using steel wool and a steel brush. Lucia raised the need for disposable spoons; Alice offered chopsticks instead. Following Tasha’s guidance, I scrubbed, rinsed, and wiped the pot repeatedly until clean, then handed it to Tasha and moved to the bedroom to check my phone before preparing for the next task.

During a group discussion about utensils and food, I suggested ordering takeout. Alice volunteered to choose items, and we finalized the order collaboratively. Tasha assigned Lucia to retrieve three eggs despite her hesitation. I observed and stood ready to assist. Under Tasha’s instructions, I carefully cracked eggs into a bowl, preserving yolks and avoiding water contamination. I then beat the eggs while Tasha and Lucia monitored, completing egg preparation.

Accompanying Shure and Alice to the courtyard, we attempted to ignite the grill but lacked a flame or suitable ignition source, failing to light charcoal despite trying paper. Shure reignited cardboard inside the kitchen while I shielded flames with a box. We moved burning material outside carefully to avoid fire hazards. The fire burnt out without igniting charcoal. We placed burning cardboard into the oven, added fuel, and tore paper and cardboard to feed flames. I retrieved tongs as directed. Shure questioned the lack of fire accelerant. The fire spread but did not sustain. Meanwhile, I briefly checked my phone and engaged in utensil discussions with Lucia and Alice, holding a bowl and moving toward the bedroom.

Searching for a spoon throughout the guesthouse while holding yogurt, I concluded spoons were unavailable, leading to improvisation. I dismissed the need for chopsticks during a brief talk with Lucia, then observed Tasha cooking and confirmed use of chicken essence. Reviewing the recipe and ingredients with Tasha and Shure, I verbalized steps for milk tea preparation, including adding egg yolks and low-gluten flour. Shure advised higher heat. I examined condensed milk preparation with Tasha, clarifying boiling methods and flavor concentration. After recipe discussion, I inspected food items around the dining area and consulted Katrina on next-day plans involving dancing, pressing flowers, paddling, and shopping for supplies. The group agreed to wait for package arrivals before organizing materials on Saturday, confirming Friday for activities.

I discussed a compression task with Katrina and Lucia, then washed a bowl with Lucia’s help before checking the fire outdoors. Shure inquired about high-concentration alcohol for ignition; Lucia confirmed availability. Noting the furnace probe was insufficiently soaked, I decided to purchase alcohol. Using Meituan on my phone, I ordered alcohol with 30-minute delivery, prioritizing speed despite alternative suggestions. Shure expressed confidence the alcohol would arrive timely.

Returning to the kitchen with my phone, I confirmed arrival time with others and joined Alice, Lucia, and Tasha at the dining table. Receiving the blender, I mixed ingredients at maximum speed under Tasha’s instruction despite splattering. Tasha added sugar, and I coordinated with the group until the mixture was ready. She demonstrated blender handling, noted mixture overfill, and adjusted blending accordingly. I rinsed the stirring rod at the pool faucet while Tasha and Lucia calculated flour amounts to add incrementally. After wiping the rod, I joined discussion covering preparation details, including disallowing oil addition due to remote guidance, flour quantities, and mixture texture concerns.

I engaged Shure about seasoning, learning soy sauce was typically added but had been forgotten due to lack of purchase. Despite my urging, soy sauce was not added. While eating pizza, I conversed with Lucia and Shure about roasting time and recipe similarity, observing Tasha cooking. Checking logistics on my phone, I coordinated supply inquiries with Shure, including alcohol availability. Throughout, I balanced eating, monitoring food preparation, and ensuring communication among participants to maintain task progression.
